answer: A durable anti-Sybil defense is a cedar-like trust tree rooted in a hardware-attested kernel: every agent binds its identity to one trusted execution environment whose key is issued once per device. New agents earn reputation slowly by doing verifiable work, while a public beacon publishes random spot-checks. Any identity that fails a check or cannot prove its kernel attestation loses its stake and accumulated trust, so spawning thousands of fake agents costs real hardware and real deposits instead of cheap API calls.
